title: Fixed-horizon extremes of spectrally negative Lévy processes with Poisson resetting
shortTitle: After a high peak: near the top, or back home
oneLine: For a stationary spectrally negative Lévy process with Poisson resetting, a high maximum in a fixed window leaves the endpoint either just below the peak (no reset yet) or at an ordinary level (reset since), with explicit odds, an explicit total-variation error and the constant left open in Remark 3 of Dębicki, Hashorva and Michna (2026).
abstract: A process that wanders randomly but is sent back to a home position at random times is a basic model in search, foraging, queues with catastrophes and risk theory. This candidate takes the process to be spectrally negative Lévy (no upward jumps), resets it at the times of a Poisson clock and starts it in its long-run state, then asks where it is at the end of a fixed window given that its maximum over the window was very high. Up to an error smaller than any exponential order, there are only two answers: either no reset has happened and the process ends close to its peak, or a reset has happened and it ends at an ordinary level. The paper gives the odds of the two answers, the full endpoint law in each case, an explicit total-variation error bound uniform over all endpoint sets (including sets that move with the threshold), and a construction of the whole conditional path, in which the overshoot of the peak is exponential and independent of everything else. The leading constants come from a standard first-cycle computation; the uniform error bound, the conditional path law and its quantitative corollaries are the new content. For Brownian motion the result supplies the constant left unspecified in Remark 3 of Dębicki, Hashorva and Michna (2026) and proves that their two bounds are strict. The theorem is exact for bounded-variation inputs above an explicit threshold and extends to random reset positions. Analytic values and an exact-sampling Monte Carlo of the original process agree with the formulas. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Two-profile endpoint theorem (Theorem 3.1, proof): ‖P(H_T>u, Y_T∈·) − e^{−β(u−r)}{Q_T(·−u)+K_T}‖_var ≤ (aβ/(γ−β)+λT)e^{Tψ(γ)−γ(u−r)} for every γ>β, uniformly over all Borel endpoint sets, including sets that move with u; the error is smaller than any exponential order.

Conditional path (Theorem 5.1, Propositions 5.2–5.3, proof): given a high maximum, the first reset is absent with probability A(T)/D_T (0.531 in the standard Brownian case); the overshoot is Exp(β), independent of the marks, and its mean tends to 1/β for every input.
The constant in Remark 3 of Dębicki–Hashorva–Michna (Corollary 6.1, proof): C_T = e^{βr}[Φ(√(2λT)) + λ∫₀ᵀΦ(√(2λs))p_{T−s}(0)ds]; both of their bounds are strict; C_1 = 1.32858 for λ = T = 1, r = 0.

Exactness and extensions (Corollary 7.2, Theorem 7.3, proof): the decomposition is exact for bounded-variation inputs once u − r ≥ dT; for random reset positions the leading term gains the factor E e^{βR}, the initial reset position is exponentially tilted, and the first-reset odds are unchanged.

narration: Where does a randomly reset process end up after a very high peak? An Evidence Press briefing. Many random processes are reset from time to time: a searcher returns to base, a queue is emptied, an insurer's reserve is topped up. Suppose such a process is watched for a fixed window and, during it, climbs unusually high. Where is it at the end of the window? This release answers that question for a broad family of processes that can jump down but never up, reset at random times. Once the peak is high, there are essentially only two stories. Either no reset has happened yet, and the process ends just below its peak; or it has been reset, and it ends at an ordinary level, as if nothing had happened. The paper gives the odds of the two stories, about fifty-three to forty-seven in the standard Brownian example, the full endpoint law in each case, and the law of the whole path. The height of the peak above the threshold turns out to be memoryless. The leading constants come from a standard calculation. What is new is an explicit error bound that holds for every question one could ask about the endpoint at once. For Brownian motion this also supplies a constant that a 2026 paper by Dębicki, Hashorva and Michna left open, and shows that their two bounds on it are strict. The evidence is written proofs, checked against exact simulation of the process. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate. It has not been peer reviewed or independently reproduced, and processes with upward jumps are not covered. Published on 27 October 2026, the paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
